I was not here during the afternoon to hear what was said about this Bill, but I have one or two papers in my hands which I would like to lay before the committee. I think, after hearing them, the committee will certainly accede to the amendment proposed, for the self-preservation of Canada. Here is a letter from Mr. Edward Murphy, a gentleman living at Prescott, and I presume well known by lion, gentlemen opposite, for he is a very strong politician and supporter of my hon. friends opposite. He writes from Prescott on the 23rd June to Mr. W. A. Lewis, barrister at Brockville. Mr. Lewis has large claims for many of the creditors. He was my opponent at the last election, and out of all the creditors who have claims against this railway company, there are only two Conservatives. However, a great portion of them are constituents of mine, and I have .always made it a rule to endeavour to represent my constituency irrespective of polities. Therefore, I take a lively interest in this Bill to see to it that these honest men who furnished the right of way, who furnished the labour by contract and so on should have their claims recognized in some way. Now, Mr. Smith writes as follows:-
Prescott, Ont., June 23rd, 1903.
W. A. Lewis, Esq.,
Barrister, &c., Brockville, Out.
Re the B. W. and S. S. M. Ry.
Dear Sir,-In 1902 I bought the bonds and stock for said road, from the Investment Company of Philadelphia, $960,000 bonds, and $960,000 stock, all the holdings of the Philadelphia people, in fact, all the holdings of bonds and stock in the United States.
In my contract for said bonds and stocks, the parties agreed to furnish the charter and all data in connection with said road, and in said contract there was no set time, nor no time limit entered into contract. I was delayed month after month waiting for the particulars and all the details in connection with the road and to this day only part of the information has been furnished as agreed, and my people urging for same during all the delay. I would beg to call your attention to my agreement with the Pacific Trust Company of New York. This is a strong company, and in Said company's charter the directors are all held personally liable for the full amounts and contracts of the company.
Re the New York German Syndicate that are now pushing for said road and trying to get charter. They are unworthy of first consideration in the matter. I was introduced to Mr. Holmes, of Holmes & Smith, and by him to Mr. Cragin, and I placed before these men proposition for said road quite fully, and they expressed a wish to enter into a contract, but informed me they could not pay the money over until they could get the bonds and realize on the bonds,

that they could sell the bonds on the New York market and handle the deal for me. This I refused and negotiated the deal with others and was adjusting the Canadian claims and getting all in line for full settlement of all judgments and outstandings against said road. During this time these usupers by misrepresentation got in league with the bondholders in Philadelphia and by using the bonds in direct opposition to the Knickerbocker Trust Company, who were the trustees of said bonds (see notice of Knickerbocker Trust Company on sale of road), and in contravention of my contract for said bonds did undertake to secure control of said bonds and to defraud the honest claims and judgments and debts against said road. They are applying for a charter to enable said syndicate to successfully rob all these honest claimants and to take over a heavily bonused road, that our government did pay as bonus to said road over $105,000 of the people's money, also the several municipalities paid $118,000 of the people's money, and at this juncture the government will surely, through the committee handling this important matter, see .that heavily bonused roads are not gobbled up by foreigners and the people defrauded out of their honest and just claims.
I placed my contract and all documents in the hands of my attorneys, Watson, Smoke & Smith, Toronto, Ont., who are going on with this matter, and I trust the committee, in their wisdom, will withhold all grants or charters for the present for extension of the road or the road now completed. Please see Trust Company's contract.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) EDWARD SMITH.

That is what Mr. Buell wrote to the Pac-fic Underwriting & Trust Company. Mr. Buell furnishes that to Mr. Smith, of Prescott, and it has been forwarded to me with authority to read it in the House. Now, here is the statement of Mr. Hervey, who was the president of the Brockville and Westport Railway Company. He formed a construction company composed of himself to build the road, and he received all the subsidies obtained from the municipalities, together with the government subsidy voted here. Mr. Hervey was here while the committee was in session, and he wrote this letter on the 20th of May, 1902. Several hon. gentlemen saw him when he was at Brockville; I think he lives in Nova Scotia now :
Re Brockville, Westport and Sault Ste. Marie Railway.
The Brockville, West.port and Sault Ste. Marie Railway Company chartered by an Act it the legislature of Ontario, entered into a contract with Robert G. Hervey for the construction and equipment of that portion of its line extending from Brockville to Westport, forty-five miles, agreeing to pay for such construction and equipment, according to schedule attached to the contract, all of the .stock, bonds and subsidies of the company.
In pursuance .of this contract, work was begun and the line .partially .completed. Rails and fastenings and the wire for fences were purchased from Cooper, Pairm&n & Co., and the Dominion Wire Company ; and a.n assignment of .the subsidy granted by the Dominion of Canada was executed by the railway company to (I think) James Cooper, of Montreal, out of which payment was to be made for such rails, fastenings and wire.
The Investment Company of Philadelphia furnished at different times certain sums of money upon notes made by the railway company and endorsed by R. G. Hervey, and with certain

bonds of the railway company as collateral security. The Investment Company of Philadelphia were familiar with the conditions and transactions of the railway company, and agreed to the assignment by the company of the Dominion subsidy for the purchase of the rails, fastenings and wire above mentioned. In July and August, 1892, an'agreement was made between Hervey and the Investment Company for the assignment by Hervey of the construction contract to the Investment Company, and thereupon Hervey endorsed such transfer upon the original contract, and the directors, who up to that time had been legally qualified by holding each the amount of stock specified in the charter and having paid all calls thereupon, resigned as such directors, and the Investment Company nominated a board of directors, who I am informed and believe have never been legally qualified as directors, and have since acted, not to represent the interests of the railway company, but as nominees of, and to carry out the wishes and instructions of the Investment Company, Hervey's object in making st;ch agreement was that the railway might be completed and equipped and the construction liabilities paid by the Investment Company, who became the contractors ; and the object cf the Investment Company was stated to be that they might acquire a good title to the stocks and bonds under the construction contract.
There were half a dozen gentlemen from Brockville who appeared before the committee who are named as directors in one of the Bills now before parliament, and I am credibly informed and believe that not a man of them has a dollar of interest in the road, and has only lent his name for the purpose of getting this legislation through parliament.
I am informed and believe that, immediately after the appointment of a new board of directors of the railway company by the in vestment Company, the assignment of the construction contract by Hervey to the Investment Company was presented to said hoard of directors, and such assignment ratified and approved by them. Instead of proceeding to complete and equip the Tailway in accordance with the terms of the contract which they then held, they failed and refused to ,pay the construction debts and to complete such construction and equipment, and I am informed and believe attempted to repudiate the assignment of the Dominion subsidy to Cooper above mentioned, and undertook to foreclose the deed of trust or mortgage securing the bonds, and several years litigation ensued ; during which time the directors of the railway company did not act in the interests of the railway company, and did not defend such foreclosure suit, as they should have none, and should have set up that the bonds held by the Investment Company should not draw interest until such contract was completed, and that the stock held by the Investment Company should not be declared fully paid until actually paid for by the completion and the equipment cf the line In accordance with the contract which they had assumed; but.in all the litigation, as I am informed and believe, the so-called directors of the railway company simply obeyed the instructions of the Investment Company.
By reason of the failure of the Investment. Company to carry out in good faith the contract they had assumed, the subsidy of the Dominion government lapsed-or at least such portion of it as had not been paid, but was wi-th-Mr. TAYLOR.
held by the government pending the completion and equipment of the line in acordauce with the specifications. I have always believed that the securities held by the Investment Company should be charged with a lien for the payment of the construction debts and the completion and equipment of the line according t.0 the contract.
Now, Mr. Hervey states that when he assigned to these people they assumed that obligation to pay these construction debts and to complete the road according to the government standard, so that Mr. Cooper could get tlie subsidy. Now, these people assumed that from Mr. Hervey, they became liable to these labourers and these creditors and liable for the completion of the road. They sold these bonds to these parties and now they come forward and repudiate the bargain made by Mr. Hervey and ask parlia-men to back them up in that and give them a charter and wipe out all these claims. These may not be legal claims against them, liut they are certainly moral claims and this government ought to recognize them. The sub-committee, as I am informed, at least the minority of the subcommittee, fully agreed and believed it was understood by the committee that they would simply legislate so as to confirm the title to the property that they had purchased and give them nothing more and nothing less. I trust that when tlie matter is fully explained and understood by lion, members on both sides of this House that the justice of our contention will be recognized and that the government will restrict the Bill to the purpose which I have mentioned, so as not to place these creditors in any worse position than they were in before the road was sold or since. I have given notice of an amendment which reads as follows :
That nothing In this Act shall prejudice the claims of the creditors in a suit now pending in the courts, to test the authority of the courts of Ontario having jurisdiction to order the sale of this railway, it being a railway for the general advantage of Canada.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at Eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
When the House took recess at six o'clock I was reading a statement made by Mr. R. G. Hervey. and I had about concluded reading it. It continues as follows :-
I have always believed that the securities held by the Investment Company should be charged with a lien for the payment of the construction debts and the completion and equipment of the line according to the contract.
While It would seem to me that .a charter should be granted permitting the extension of this railway, it does seem to me only reasonable and fair that such charter should provide for 'he payment within a certain time of the debts incurred under the construction contract which

was assumed by the Investment Company ; or possibly it might be made a condition of the charter that any subsidy that might hereafter be granted by either the Dominion or provincial governments should be charged wiith the payment thereout of the money coming to Cooper (whose security was destroyed by the acts of the Investment Company), and also for the payment thereout of a sum sufficient to settle the other indebtedness incurred under said construction contract, and that the charter should be contingent thereupon and should lapse at an agreed time if such liabilities-which should long ago have been paid by the Investment Company, as above mentioned-were not satisfied.
The above is an accurate statement.
(Signed) ROBT. G. HERVEY. Now, Mr. Chairman, the committee is seized with all the facts in reference to this railway. My hon. friend from Cornwall (Mr. Pringle) has read to the House the action that was taken by this parliament in the cases of the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo Railway Company and the Northwest Central Railway Company, and the Hereford Railway Company, in which cases hon. gentlemen opposite supported a proposal similar to that which we make now. When these companies applied to' parliament for extended powers, parliament granted their charters only on condition that the just claims against them should be paid. I am satisfied that now that parliament is aware of the facts in this case, parliament will not perpetuate an injustice against the creditors of this road. One of these creditors, a Mr. Knowlton, who appeared before the committee, furnished a right of way, and although he never gave a title, the road took possession of it, and he has never received a cent. Besides that he has a claim under a contract for construction, the whole amounting to $8,000 or $10,000. I am sure that parliament will not legislate that gentleman out of his just rights. I am glad to see the hon. gentleman for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) coming into the House, because in the case of the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo Railway he moved an amendment in favour of the creditors of that road, and I am glad to say it was adopted by the House. I am sure that his voice will he raised now on behalf of the creditors of the Brockville, Westport and Sault Ste. Marie Railway Company. I ask the Minister of Labour to see that labouring men who worked for days and months on this railway, and who never received a dollar of wages, will be protected now that parliament can protect them. I also ask that in any legislation that is granted, it shall he provided that it will in no way interfere with the case that is now pending in the courts. It is the duty of the government to look to all legislation passing through this House, and I trust they will take measures to see that justice is done to the creditors of this company.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I would like to say a word on behalf of one of my constituents who has
a claim against this company for $5,000, for money that has actually gone into the construction of this road. A company was chartered by this parliament to build this road, and in the building of that road they incurred certain expenses for labour and material, and the company being in default the road was sold under an order of the court, and practically the same company bought it in.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: That is wrong. I may state that the sub-committee had six statutory declarations before them to the contrary". One company had no connection with the other.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: It makes no difference whether the same men bought it in or not; some one bought the road with its rights and liabilities, as I understand it.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Excuse me.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: They should have done so.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: You evidently do not understand the character of a sale under a mortgage of bonds.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: 'Well, I do understand that a certain number of men bought this road in a court sale, and so far as that sale is concerned the purchasers were relieved from liability for the claims that were against the road that were not included in their claims. These people got what they bought, that is what they paid for, and that is all that is coming to them. We had no responsibility with regard to that matter, but they were not satisfied with what they bought, and they come back to this parliament and ask for something further from parliament. They ask for certain extension of time and certain extension of authority.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: That is wrong ; read the Bill. ,

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
These people who bought the road come to parliament and ask certain powers and authority, beyond what they obtained by the purchase of the road. I have been a member of this parliament for some seven years and scarcely a session has gone by that there has not been a similar case in which the liens against a railroad have been maintained against the company applying to parliament. During this verv session our friends from Bona-venture "(Mr. Marcil) and from Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) have maintained the rights of their constituents in regard to certain railroads in these counties. I am not prepared to say what was the actual result, hut I am certain that the committee upheld the contention of these hon. gentlemen. I remember some years ago when the member for Lincoln maintained a similar contention in regard to a railway in his county, and he was supported in his contention by the House. It was a perfectly fair contention

to my mind, that the labour and material which actually constructs a road should be a lien against that road, and when the opportunity occurs to enforce that lien, when legislation is before parliament, that is the time to see that justice is done. There is no manner of doubt that this road owes certain people honest money. There is no doubt that the company which under an Act of this parliament is going to own the road is given certain privileges by this parliament because of the existence of that road which the money and the labour of these men have actually constructed. It seems to me utterly unfair that these people should be allowed to have the benefit of this money and of this labour without being compelled to give value for it. We are giving them power to raise money. Then, I think the first thing we should do is to compel them to pay the money which the enterprise they have acquired actually and properly owes. As to the account which I have mentioned, a matter of $5,000, it is possibly the man's whole fortune, and it seems to me a terrible thing if people can be actually swindled as in this case. I do not care if it is done under the colour of law or under the procedure of the courts, it is robbery just the same ; the result is just the same. It seems to me that it is the privilege of parliament, if it is not its duty, to protect the rights of innocent parties who have put their money and labour into the construction of the road; and it is a privilege which I for one will certainly exercise, so far as I have the power.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Yale and Cariboo (Mr. Galliher) asked the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) to look at the Bill. That is just what I would like to do-see a copy of the Bill as it has been presented by a majority of the sub-committee.
I think in all fairness to the members of the House this Bill should be printed before we proceed further with it. There is not a member of the House who knows anything about the Bill. As I have seen it in the hands of the chairman, it grants these gentlemen more powers than they purchased. It grants them the power to change the name.	.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: It would help the creditors a lot to keep the old name, wouldn't it ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: It would not do them anj harm. Their claims are against the Brock ville, Westport and Sault Ste. Marie Railway Company.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: How will the change of name affect them ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not know whether it will or not ; but there is an action pend Ing against that company. Then the lion member for Yale and Cariboo says that the parties who bought the road are not the bondholders. How does he know that ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Not because I have written statements from men, but because I have statutory declarations which mean something, whereas letters are matters which anybody can write.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman has them, will he produce them ?

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: They were before the sub-committee.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I attended every meeting of the sub-committee and I never heard of them. If my hon. friend has them, let them be read, so that they will be placed in ' Hau-sard,' where we can see them.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I have them here.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend send one of them over to me ? I believe the evidence is just as strong that the investment company who took the assignment from Mr. Hervey subject to all these claims are Interested in the purchase of the road. They handed the bonds over to the parties at a nominal price, and these parties appeared in their own names and persons, and made the purchase, and paid in the bonds which they held as the purchase money, thereby barring any other person from purchasing unless he came forward with a sufficient amount of money to pay the bonds in full. I am satisfied ini my own mind, and it was stated by the lawyers who appeared before the sub-committee, Messrs. Hutcheson and Fisher and Mr. Lewis, thatl these parties purchased for the investment company.
I will produce Mr. Hervey's affidavit corroborating the letter he wrote, and Mr. Smith's affidavit corroborating his statement, if the committee will allow me a couple of days' time to get them. If my hon. friend will produce the affidavits he speaks of, I will produce affidavits in a short time contradicting them.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: We often say it is a right duty of parliament to protect vested rights ; but in passing this Bill, instead of respecting and protecting vested rights, we are practically confiscating those rights.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: What about the men who paid their money for the railway at a public sale ?

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Let them have what they bought.
Mr. GiiiiLIIIER. That is all they are asking.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: We have not refused to confirm their purchase, and that is all that parliament can be fairly asked to do without tacking on conditions. I say that we are not respecting vested rights; we are doing what parliament has always been advised it should never do-interfering with and destroying vested rights.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Tust a word in answer to what my hon. friend has said. If he

understood the principle of foreclosing either a mortgage or bonds or anything of that kind, he would realize the absolute nonsense of what he is saying. We all know that if a piece of property is mortgaged, and I am the first mortgagee, and there are other mortgages subsequent to mine, and other judgments and claims subsequent, and if there is default made in the first mortgage, all the parties are brought in, as they were in this case. Their claims are mentioned in the report of the master ; they are there to prove their claims either in person or by representation. The master orders a sale of the property. The purchaser may be an entirely different party from either the mortgagee or the mortgagor or any of the subsequent encumbrances. If his bid buys the property, he gets it at that bid, unless some of the other parties are prepared to overbid him. That is where they have their protection ; they can, if they want to, overbid him sufldciently to cover their claims. When the hon. member for East Grey talks about parliament taking away vested rights, 1 ask him, if people attend a public sale ordered by the court, and buy the property, I do not care whether they have bought it at its full value or al half its value, have they no vested rights ?

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Is there not litigation now pending in regard to the validity of the sale ?

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I will tell you what the litigation is that is pending. There was a report from the master as to the distribution of the purchase money. From that report the late James Cooper made an appeal. The hearing of that appeal was set for the 23rd of April, 1903. The appeal was heard, and judgment was given on the 25th of April, dismissing the appeal with costs. There has been an appeal taken which we who practice law understand the effect of. which takes the matter over vacation. It cannot be heard until the long vacation is over, and the intention is to cause delay in order to obstruct this Bill. But that appeal does not affect the title. The courts had already decided that, these bonds had priority over all the other creditors. That decision was appealed against and Mr. Cooper was defeated.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I will put my hon. friend right with reference to the appeal now pending. It is an appeal as to whether the courts of Ontario had jurisdiction to sell a Dominion road ?

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Has not that already been decided ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: No, no decision has been rendered.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: It is merely a question of appeal from beginning to end.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: If there is absolutely nothing in that appeal, what isMlie objection to make this Bill subject- to the decision on that appeal ?

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The objection is this. I did not intend to go into this question at all until we came to it on the particular clause in that Bill, but from the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite they propose to go over and over the same ground on every clause of the Bill. What do the amendments of the hon. member for Leeds amount to. He has been posing here as the friend of the workingman, let us see what assistance his amendments would be to the workingman. The first amendment is that the words 1 North-western' be struck out, and the words ' Sault Ste Marie ' inserted in its place. If he can find any advantage to the workingman in doing that, I should like to know what it is. The second amendment is to strike out ' $500,000 ' and substitute * $160,000 ' so as to make the capitalization $160,000 instead of $500,000. How is that going to help the workingman ? His third amendment is that section eight, declaring the. railway to be for the general advantage of Canada, be struck out. But, if there is any advantage to the workingman, it will rather be found on leaving that section in the Bill than in striking it out. His fourth amendment provides that section nine be amended so that the proceeds of the bonds shall only be used for the completion and the equipment and betterment of the forty-five miles of road. How is that going to help the workingman ? Not one particle. Here is the only amendment that could possibly be of any benefit to the workingman. It is an amendment providing that when the railway is completed and passes government inspection, should parliament see fit to renew [DOT] the subsidy, that subsidy will be paid over to the estate of the late James Cooper. But, the subsidy had already been assigned to Mr. Cooper ; and if he has any rights under that assignment, these rights still exist. If the subsidy is to be revoted, I am not sure that the assignment would not still hold good ; but if the contrary opinion should be held, every opportunity would be given the parties interested to be reheard on the subject. Why should we anticipate legislation on an event which may never happen ? But would that pay the workingman, whom my hon. friend is so solicitous about, and whom I would like to see paid just as well as any hon. member in this House ? Not at all. It will pay James Cooper.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Read the next section.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The next is an amendment to section twelve which provides that should the company apply to parliament at any time for further powers

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: That is just what they are doing now.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
No, this has reference to a future application. It provides that

should they apply to parliament at any time for further powers, parliament shall inquire into certain claims. You are asking parliament to legislate against itself by declaring that if at any time this company should come to it, it would be bound to do something. And all you want it to do is to make an inquiry into these claims. The amendment does not require the company to pay these claims. What different position then would the creditors be in than they are now ? Supposing this Bill should pass as it stands, surely the creditors are just in as good a position to come to parliament, when this company is asking for further extension, as they would be if you had inserted a clause of that nature in this Bill. We are not taking anything away from the creditors. We are not asking them to waive their rights in anyway, and the insertion of a clause of that description would not add one iota to their benefit. Then section thirteen provides that nothing in this Act shall prejudice the claims of creditors. Then there is the amendment to add section thirteen and provides that nothing in this Bill shall prejudice the claims of creditors in a suit now pending, to test the authority of the courts of Ontario. Why should it be necessary to put in any such clause. You are asking us to provide against some thing which does not exist. You are asking us to provide against a contingency which cannot possibly happen. What difference would it make if you had that clause in ? These are the proposed amendments of the hon. member for Leeds. There is not one of them which will tend to bring the workingman one iota nearer his pay. There has been a little cross firing and certain assertions have been made with regard to this sub-committee. I cannot speak as to all that took place in the sub-committee, because I only attended two of the meetings. One of them happened to be the last. With that draft report of the sub-committee I had nothing to do. I have not seen it up to the present, therefore my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy), although he looked pretty hard at me when he insinuated that tliat_ report was not exactly what it ought to be, is completely at fault. I had nothing to do with the report and I am satisfied that in the hands of the Chairman, it was in the hands of a gentleman who would not do anything except what he understood to be the wish of the majority of the committee.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: My hon. friend has accused me of insinuating "that the report was tampered with ?

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I understood from the hon. gentleman's demeanour that he thought T had something to do with it.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I want to make myself clear to the hon. gentleman. I neither insinuated, nor am I conscious that my demeanour was such as to insinuate. AVhat 1 did say, and I still say it, was that the

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: lion, gentleman wabbled a little on the matter before the committee.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: After the explanation of the l\on. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) I beg leave to apologize for having anything to say in the matter. Now, as to the action of this sub-committee, it was said by some hon. gentlemen opposite, particularly by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) that the sub-committee had neglected part of their duties-or words to that effect-in not going into these creditors' claims. Let me inform my hon. friend that the sub-committee did go into the question and heard parties with regard to these claims. But the majority of the committee thought that that was a matter hat had better be left to the Committee of the House or to the House to deal with when these claims should be presented if any application was made for a subsequent extension.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Galliher) will allow me-that is exactly our contention. But we ask, why was it not put in the report ? If the report will come down in the shape in which the matter was agreed upon in the committee, then, so far as I am concerned, I am perfectly satisfied. And if the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Harty) says that was not agreed upon, and that the report in its present form is the correct report, I will accept his statement so far as I am individually concerned!.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: And without the chairman's sanction to what I say, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pringle) will not accept it ?

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: If the hon. member for Kingston who was chairman of the subcommittee and in whom I have every confidence says that the report as now in the hands of the clerk is the agreement of that committee I accept it at once. But I am satisfied that he will not say so. It was a majority vote.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The question was discussed in the sub-committee whether we should report making the statement that we bad considered these claims. I think two of the committee, a minority, wished this put in, but the majority decided they would notput it in. Therefore, the report as decided upon by the majority did not contain that limitation. I state that as a fact, because I was there; and I hope the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pringle) will accept it. But whether be does or not that is the truth of the matter. When these clauses come up one by one, I shall be prepared to discuss these matters at greater length. In the meantime, I felt that I could not allow the representation as to the general character of the transaction that has been made and so strongly urged by hon. members opposite to go without placing this committee in possession of the facts. It has also been stated that certain

propositions were made by Mr. Barwick and by one of the parties applying for this legislation whose name is in the charter.
X can only say that such offers were not made at either of the meetings at which 1 was present. If hon. gentlemen who were at these committee meetings say that such was the case, I certainly accept their word for it. But, speaking generally on this Bill, I point out that these people only came here asking for a confirmation of their purchase. But, surely hon. members would not expect a Bill of this kind simply to confirm such a purchase and give them the bonding privilege of $10,000 a mile. Objection should not be taken to the other clauses here, which are such clauses as appear in an ordinary incorporation-such as the names and adres-ses of the parties, who shall be provisional directors, capital stock, head office of the company, and so on.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I wish to say a few words as to

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I am anxious to hear the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) on this Bill.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Well, I hope that the hon. minister's ambition will be satisfied.
I have been anxious for a long time to ascertain the interest the hon. gentleman (Mr. Galliher) was taking on behalf of the poor labourers who built this forty-five miles of road. I have been equally anxious to know what position' the Minister of Labour (Hon. Sir William Mulock) took upon it. The hon. gentleman from Yale and Cariboo (Mr. Galliher) said that tlie sale was made by order of the court under mortgage and there was no appeal. If so, what are these people here for ? They have appealed to the highest court in the empire in these matters. This court of parliament deals with legal claims, with claims of equity and with moral claims, and to this court these people have appealed. All we ask is that this court should settle this case on the same lines as they have settled other similar cases, that this court shall observe a well established precedent. We can confirm this purchase, but, in doing so, we can protect the rights that have not been protected by the court from which the hon. gentleman says there is no appeal.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I am very happy to gratify my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) by giving him my views on this question, and I hope he will accept my thanks for his giving me the pleasure of hearing him. It is a rare treat, and I appreciate it accordingly. With reference to the claims of the workingmen, I quite agree with all the hon. members of this committee, that it is most desirable, in all cases where it is at all possible, that these claims should be properly protected. I was not present at the discussion of this matter in the Railway
Committee, therefore, I have no information on the subject except from what has transpired in this debate. I understand the facts to be as follows : That this railway company having become financially involved, the road was offered for sale by public auction under a decree of the court and was sold free from all encumbrances to the highest bidder. The purchaser became owner of it free from all claims. It is now urged that the purchasers, although they have obtained a title to the property free from all claims, shall nevertheless be compelled to pay some unpaid sums of money owing to the workingmen, for labour I suppose, in the construction of operation of the road. Now, the purchasers have acquired the property free from all claims.
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock).

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit me-the hon. gentleman has repeated again and again ' free from all claims.' If the hon. gentleman will look into the case he will find that it was not free from such claims as might be adjudged; against it by the court.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I have not got the advertisement here, I suppose the advertisement has been before the Railway Committee. My hon. friend from Yale and Cariboo (Mr. Galliher) has stated that the property was sold by the court to the highest bidder, and there was no condition in the contract of sale stating that the purchaser was to acquire the property subject to any existing claims. If there was no such condition in the purchase the purchasers acquired the property free from all claim. Such is the law. When property is offered for sale and there is no stipulation that the purchase should be subject to existing claims or liens of any kind, then the presumption is that it has been sold free from all encumbrances ; that is the law of the land. If there is no such a stipulation or reservation of this kind, then the purchasers acquired the right to the property free from all encumbrances, all outstanding claims of any kind.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Well. I will not enter into a controversy with my hon. friend on the subject, the law is too plain to be subject to controversy. In the . province of Ontario the law is beyond all question that when a property is offered for sale by public auction and there is no state; ment in the conditions of sale that the pur' chaser, in addition to paying his purchase money, shall have to pay other claims, or ' take the property subject to other claims, he . is entitled to the property free from all en-; cumbrances. There is no legal gentleman of ; any standing in the province of Ontario who [ will controvert that proposition for one mo. ment.
; Mr. PRINGLE. Will the hon. gentleman r permit me to ask him a question ? Is this

parliament bound to do anything more than to ratify and confirm that purchase 1 That is the first question. Are we as a parliament bound to do anything more than to ratify and confirm that purchase, subject to any rights in existing litigation ?

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: No applicant to parliament has a legal right to legislation, all will concede that. It is always in the discretion of parliament to grant or refuse legislation that is asked for. But it is a novel proposition that parliament is to become a collector of debts and to sell its legislation-for that is what is proposed here.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is not answering my question. I do not quite agree with him in the statement he makes. I think we are bound under the Railway Act to ratify and confirm that purchase if application is made to this parliament, as it should be, within a year. But having done that, are we as a parliament bound to do anything more for this company ? Let me continue a little further ? If I am right and if we are not bound to do anything more than to ratify and confirm that purchase, and if this company then comes and asks for large privileges, have we not a right as a parliament to ask them to deal equitably with these claims, if we think there are merits in these claims ?	,

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
They have a right to ask for legislation, but for us to withhold legislation because what we ask for is not conceded, is a very different proposition. I do not think it is a wise procedure for parliament to put a price upon its legislation, as is proposed. I will tell my hon. friend where I think the mistake arose. This railway company, as I understand, received a large subsidy from the Dominion parliament. I have turned up the statute of 1894 and I find there a grant of a subsidy of something over $80,000, and a reference is made to a statute of 1880 granting a subsidy as well. I do not know the extent of these subsidies, but it is conceded in this debate that a considerable amount of public money in the way of subsidy has gone into the construction of this road. Now it would have been a very simple matter for the government of tlnit day to protect the workingmen. They could have stipulated in the contract under which they allowed that subsidy to be earned that it should not be paid out until proof of the payment of the wages of the men. They had a very simple remedy, they have not apparently chosen to avail themselves of that opportunity. They have paid the subsidy over to the company without first seeing that the workingmen were paid. There was an easy remedy in their own hands. But my hon. friends opposite, instead of resting the responsibility for the loss to the workingmen where it belongs, upon the government of Mr. PRINGLE.
that day, that omitted to take up the interests of the workingmen and protect them -instead of placing the responsibility where it belongs, they now seek to make the purchaser who has acquired this property, pay a debt for which he is not responsible. An infinitely fairer proposition would be for the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) to propose that the members of parliament themselves should contribute towards the payment of that debt. I understand that the amount of wages owing to the workingmen is some $6,000. If we are going to pay that debt out of other people's money, had we not better first show our generosity by paying it out of our own money 'i It is a simple thing for us to be very generous here, to sit down and by legislation vote to pay a certain debt out of another man's property ; but it would be far more creditable to us, and give greater proof of real generosity of spirit, if we were to contribute our percentage of the money ourselves. Let my hon. friend from Leeds make that proposition in parliament. I am sure he will receive the assent of his own friends, they are burning with eagreness to pay these bills; perhaps we should be equally generous on this side, and the whole question would be solved. But instead of that, what does the hon. member propose ? The hon. member for Yale and Cariboo a few moments ago read the proposed amendments. One of these amendments, number H, is as follows:
That when 'the said company completes the said railway sio that it will pass government inspection and be 'entitled to receive the unearned subsidy, should the parliament of Canada see fit to revate it, it having lapsed, that it be paid over to the estate of the late James Cooper, who had an assignment of the said subsidy as security for rails supplied to equip the road.
Now, if he is sincerely desirous of aiding the workingmen, why does he not first of all ask that this unearned subsidy be applied in payment of these workingmen ? Why does he come here and ask that whatever money is realized must first be banded over to the merchants who sold the rails ? Why does he not consider that the workingmen should be entitled to the first claim ? If we are going to take a sum of money that is not under the control of this parliament and distribute it amongst persons, surely his sympathy should fii-st go forth to the workiDgmen. I ask him why he does not move that that fund be first charged with the payment of the wages before he hand it over to the payment for these rails ? Now, another feature occurs to me. If notwithstanding the court ordering the sale of the property free from all encumbrances, parliament Is going to intervene and prevent tlie purchasers deriving the full value of their purchase, we are going to discredit sales, and we are going to depreciate the value of property that is to be sold. If it is known generally that any property, that is the subject of legislation by this

parliament will not pass to the purchaser though he buys it under conditions that gave him a full title in fee simple, free from encumbrance, if, notwithstanding that fact, we, by our practice, sqy that any company becoming the purchaser of such property that may apply to parliament for legislation shall not be entitled to the fruit of its purchase, we violate the law of contract, and destroy the value of sales held under the law of the land. The proposition in this case seems to me utterly devoid of merit. The blame rests with the late government in not having hedged around the public grant of money with conditions not entitling the company to receive the money until they had done justice to their workingmen. That condition was not put in where it would have been effective and this trouble has come from the neglect of the late government and hon. gentlemen who supported that government come here now seeking with professions of interest to try and get recovery when they know full well that they have no equity here, to-day, when they know full well that they have no legal claim, and who are attempting to make use of this parliament by coercion to wring money out of people who are entitled to fair consideration, and to persuade this high court of parliament to prevent them from getting that consideration except they submit to what is an unjust levy of taxation or to be deprived of legislation which is fairly their due. Let the merits of the application be discussed fully and fairly without importing the condition that the petitioners coming to this parliament may be compelled as a consideration for getting legislation to which they may otherwise be entitled to that shall contribute moneys for claims such as these. It is a degredation of parliament, a lowering of the object of parliament, and it is asking parliament to lend itself to a violation of the rights of the people. In our desire to befriend people we must be just. There is a higher obligation than merely a wish to be kind to people. There is the highest of all obligations-the obligation of being just and not adopting a confiscatory policy such as is involved in this proposal.

Marie Railway, because the law says that if a railway changes hands the new purchasers must come to parliament to get the purchase confirmed. I was not present in the Railway Committee and neither were the members whom I had named on the subcommittee, and yet the Railway Committee refused to let the matter stand. The Bill is now before the House in its mutilated state with recommendations which the minority of the sub-committee say they did not agree to. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Galliher) has affidavits from these gentlemen stating that they are not the same as the original company, let him read them, because both the member for Hamilton and the member for Cornwall say that these affidavits were not produced in the committee at any time they were present. The creditors are quite willing that parliament should simply confirm what these people purchased, leaving the name of the railway as it was when they purchased it. They paid $160,000 for the road, and parliament should make that the capital stock instead of increasing it to $500,000. The third amendment is that section 8 be struck out and that was not considered necessary, because the original charter says that the road is for the general advantage of Canada. We are simply called upon to confirm the sale here, and we need not give them any bonding privileges at all, but when parliament does undertake to give them extended privileges these creditors say that this company will never want any further legislation and that now is the time to get their rights protected and justice done them. I am willing to put the bonding privileges at $10,000 a mile, with the provision that when these bonds are sold the proceeds will go for the betterment of the road. If the government will accept my proposition simply to confirm the purchase ; to leave the name of the road as it was, to make the capital stock $160,000 and to give them a bonding privilege of $10,000 per mile, it will put the creditors in the same position as they were before the road was bought, and I will withdraw my objections.

When we see these Americans coming here asking for a great franchise we should take care that our poor Canadian people are protected. Why should you grant to these people something that this parliament has no rigut to grant, and why should you refuse to protect the poor Canadians who have claims against this road ? Let me tell the Minister of Labour that I have been here for twenty-one years and that I have never heard of a case similar to this in which it was refused to incorporate in a similar Bill the conditions which we now ask to be incorporated. The Minister of Labour takes different ground now. He says : these people bought this road and they are coming for a charter ; they are Americans and we must give them all they ask for ; we can pay no attention to the poor labouring men wlio have claims against this road. And yet the Minister of Labour professes to be the friend of the workingmen of this country. If he is let him simply confirm the sale to these Yankees, and let him protect the rights of our own people. The validity of that sale is being tested now in the courts as to whether the province of Ontario had the right to sell a Dominion road. Let me ask the Postmaster General why he is giving to these Americans who bought that road for $160,000 the power to capitalize the stock at $500,000 ? The sub-committee agreed that the bonding privilege should be $10,000 and that the proceeds of the sale of the bonds should be put into the road but there is not a word about that in the report of the sub-committee.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has not asked us to do anything yet. I do not find any motion of his before the House asking us not to grant this legislation except on condition of the workingmen being paid. But he has not yet answered my question. Permit me to explain what I understand to be the practice in connection with the granting of railway subsidies. Parliament grants railway subsidies by an Act which contains the provision that these subsidies shall be payable to the railways named according to the terms of the contract entered into between the government and the company. It therefore remains for the government of the day to include in the contract such conditions as they may deem proper in connection with the granting of the subsidy. I ask my hon. friend to explain if he can why the government that was in power when the subsidies of 1889, 1S92 and 1894 were granted, did not stipulate that the company should ' pay the workingmen. If they did not include such a very reasonable provision in the contract, it is rather late in the day for the hon. gentleman now to discover the default. Again, I ask him if he thinks the workingmen should be paid, why has he not given notice of an amendment to that effect? Instead of that, he proceeds to argue, why should we grant legislation of this kind'to American citizens? Well, I think all men are equal before the law, no matter what their nationality is. When any man acquires a legal right, be he rich or poor, Canadian, British subject or foreigner, his rights before the courts of Canada are equal. I should be ashamed to hear any other doctrine maintained on the floor of the parliament of Canada, and I am sorry that my hon. friend should come down to such an appeal as that. My hon. friend says that in all other cases when railway companies which have been in default have applied for legislation, conditions requiring them to pay the wages they owed have been imposed. I would draw a distinction between a company which is in default

and a purchaser of a property, as in this case. If the old original company had remained in the ownership of its former owners, and they were applying here for legislation, we could very well say to them, you owe your workingmen, and we insist upon your paying them. Perhaps that was the case in the other instance which the hon. gentleman has cited. But in this instance the whole property has been sold just as effectually as if it were a farm; and what would one think of a purchaser of a farm at public auction, free from all debts and claims, being afterwards asked to pay debts owing by the farmer to his farm hands ? It would be equally unreasonable to compel the purchasers of this property, who had purchased it free from all claims, to pay claims they had never agreed to pay-to hold them up, as the hon. gentleman puts it in his graphic way. It is not the duty of parliament to hold up these men, and I am sure that the workingmen of Canada would repudiate such a suggestion. I am sure that the hon. gentleman has not the approval of the workingmen of Brockville for his suggestion that we should hold up these men and compel them to pay what they are not legally liable to pay. If they are legally liable to pay, why does not the hon. gentleman liave them proceeded against by law?

As a matter of civil rights, the right of way is under the jurisdiction of the province of Ontario.

concern, the purchaser has the right, for a certain time, a year or so, to make use of the old powers.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
