maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I do not think the hon. Minister of Labour thoroughly understands the position. If he did, I am satisfied he would agree witn the minority. Let me briefly tell him the position. Three Bills came before the Railway Committee. The first was Bill (No. 67), which was promoted by the creditors, asking for incorporation as a railway company, under the name of the Brockville and Western Railway Company, for the purpose of building a line from Westport to Sault Ste. Marie. Under the terms of that Bill, the applicants agreed to deposit in the hands of the Minister of Railways and Canals, in the event of their obtaining this charter, $50,000 to be divided relatively among the creditors, including the wage-earners. Then there was the application, Bill (No. 89) of certain other gentlemen asking for incorporation for a railway. Then there was the Bill under discussion, (No. 104) asking for the ratification of this purchase. I agree with the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals that we should grant to these people, irrespective of their nationality, just what they are entitled to. But I submit that parliament is the highest tribunal in our land and that when these people come to us and ask us to ratify and confirm the purchase they have made, if we think any injustice has been done, we have a perfect right to see that it is remedied. These people know when they make the purchase that they cannot buy that franchise, that no Ontario court has power to give them an absolute title to the franchise, and that they have got to come to this parliament in order to get their purchase ratified and confirmed. The view we took in the subcommittee was this. There were seven supporters of the government in that committee and four members from this side ? We found that we could not come to any agreement by which these workingmen or these contractors would be protected, and we took the view that we were bound to give these people a Bill ratifying and confirming their purchase, but we were not bound to go any further. And, if I understand it, what we wanted was a report to the effect that these Bills were thrown out; that there would simply be a Bill ratifying and confirming that sale, and, in the event of either party at a later stage applying for privileges from



this parliament, the question of these claims could be discussed.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Might I interject a remark ? Was it not the feeling in that subcommittee, at least on the part of those who were there at the last meeting, when I was there-and I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pringle), also-that there should be a clause giving them certain bonding privileges on account of the very bad state in which the road was, and on account of the danger to trains occasioned by that condition, and so it being in the interest of the public generally that they should be allowed to issue bonds so as to be able to put the road in a proper state ? Was not that the general feeling of the sub-committee ?

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Is that the whole of the question ?

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I was not present at the final meeting of the sub-committee. Had I been, I should certainly have made a strong effort to have the report put in proper shape. But I understand the gentlemen who formed the minority made a strong fight to have a condition put in the report that if bonding privileges were given the proceeds of the bonds should be applied to the betterment of the road.
large concessions, such as there are in this Bill, they should be required to do what is equitable to the creditors. The lion. Minister of Labour, in his very strong effort to deprive these people of any possibility of getting their wages, has made the statement that once the courts foreclosed that mortgage, there was no possible remedy for the workmen. This parliament, the highest tribunal in our land has the authority and the power to ascertain if an undertaking such as a railway has paid its debts ; 'and if debts are still owing, it has the power to make the payment of them a condition of legislation. In a recent judgment in the Supreme Court of the United States, Mr. Justice Brewer, one of the' most eminent jurists in the states, in a judgment with reference to the foreclosure of mortgages on railways, declared that the Supreme Court had long since recognized that under present conditions circumstances may arise under which the question is more than one between mortgager and mortgagee, and that the peculiar conditions of the railway situation justified the court in entertaining pleas for priority of some claims over the debt secured by mortgage. Who is foreclosing the mortgage in this case ? Is it not the Philadelphia Investment Company, and is it not true that this company agreed with Mr. R. G. Hervey that these claims

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The latter part is right, but they were not opposed to the giving of the bonding privilege to the extent of $10,000 per mile.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Certainly not. But it was on condition that the bonds were to be used in the improvement of the road. As I pointed out this afternoon, this road really cost the purchasers less than $100,000. They are asking the privilege of bonding for $450,000 besides issuing stock for a very large amount. What do they want these bonding privileges for unless for the betterment and improvement of the road ? And that is the condition we desire to put in the Bill.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: But surely my hon. friend (Mr. Pringle) will not deny that if you attach such conditions to a bonding "privilege as to compel the purchaser of these bonds to see to the application of the money, it will make the sale of the bonds impossible. To impose such a condition would be to defeat the very object of bonding.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: But we are getting away from the point I desire to confine myself to. I said that the sub-committee found that there was some $10,000 owing to workmen, and we felt that if there was any way to protect these workmen we should endeavour to find it. We felt that we should hardly be justified in refusing the applicants a Bill to ratify and confirm their purchase, but we felt also that if we granted them

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The decision of Mr. Justice Brewer does not apply to this case. If I followed the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Pringle) reading properly, the question referred to was as between different classes of creditors, the court might give priority to one over another, just as in a case of salvage. But the case is different here. A new party appears on the scene in the purchaser.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Let me say in answer to the Minister of Labour (Hon. Sir William Muloek) that the new party who appears here, I think it has been shown pretty conclusively, are simply the creature of the Philadelphia Investment Company, that the Philadelphia Investment Company have simply taken this means of acquiring the property and realizing their money. When we look at the merits, we find that Robert G. Hervey had the contract for the construction of the road, he receiving all the bonds and all the stock. When he was not able to complete the road, he transferred the bonds and the stock to the Philadelphia Investment Company, they agreeing to pay the debts of these wage-earners. They ran the road at a profit for several years. The receiver lias in hand a surplus of some $lo,-000 which the Investment Company had taken. Then they take proceedings to foreclose their mortgage. I say the equities are strongly with the creditors in this case. We are not asking for anything unreasonable, we are not asking that a clause be

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
inserted in a Bill that these wage-earners should be protected but we said that if all these Bills were put on one side, let a report be made that if these people come before parliament at a future time and ask for large powers, then, the creditors would have the right to come before parliament and press their claims. But, in the position in which it is put at the present time, it will simply put an end to the creditors having any sort of chance of obtaining redress. Now, the hon. Minister of Labour makes the same contention as the promoters of the syndicate Bill, which is that the question of equity in favour of the labourers and those who supplied the material does not exist in this case, because the syndicate made a purchase at a court sale. X submit that this reason does not apply. Why ? Because the conditions of the sale were unreasonable, and were framed with the object in view of a large bondholder becoming a purchaser. I presume that these creditors were parties to that suit. I suppose the court advertised for creditors, and that these wage-earners and contractors proved their claims. If so, they were before the court, and parties to the record, and if the conditions were unreasonable, they had their remedy of pointing that out, and asking the court to impose reasonable conditions. Do I understand the Minister of Labour to take the position that this parliament is bound not only to ratify ,and confirm that purchase, but to grant to .these applicants all privileges and concessions that they may wish for without at all asking them to make some concession towards the men who put their money into that enterprise? Is that the position the Minister of Labour takes?
. The POSTMASTER GENERAL. I do not see where these purchasers have assumed any liabilities towards the creditors in question. They are purchasers in the ordinary sense of the word, so far as I know, they have been so found by the court. .They buy the property free from all claim. I would be just as pleased as my hon. friend or any one else to see the workingmen get their pay, but I do not see any legal or moral ground on which we can compel the *purchasers of the property to pay claims (for which they never became liable, the .payment of which they did not assume, and *which they are entirely free from by the order of the court.
. Mr. PRINGLE. Let me ask another question? Are we legally or morally bound to give to these applicants who purchased a road for about $100,000, bonding power for $450,000 ?
. The POSTMASTER GENERAL. It is quite within the discretion of parliament to *grant such legislation or to withhold it, as *in its wisdom it sees fit to do; but it must 234J
proceed on some recognized principles in granting or withholding the legislation. The hon. member for Leeds says parliament can hold the applicants up and withhold from them the moral rights of petitioners.ro appeal to parliament, simply in order to levy blackmail upon them. You would not want parliament to be a party to a thing like that.
* Mr. PRINGLE. Let me ask the hon. gentleman this : Is it not quite within the discretion of parliament in granting a concession to these applicants to say to them, We find that certain moneys were invested in *that road, certain labour has gone into that iroad which has not been paid for, and if you are to get the privilege of bonding that road for $10,000 a mile, we in our discretion ask you to do what is equitable and right with these claims? That surely is *within our discretion, parliament has done it on other occasions. When the hon. gentleman takes the position that there should be no saving clause in this Bill, we are *assuming that there should be a saving Clause in regard to litigation. I may say to him that Mi'. Barwiek, who represented (these applicants, conceded at once that there *should be a saving clause in. regard to litigation. Now, let me tell him that litigation is now on hand in following particulars : In the foreclosure of the Philadelphia Investment Company, of the Brockville, Westport and Sault Ste. Marie Railway Company, there is an appeal from the master's final report. This appeal is set down for bearing at the next sitting of the division court. Would not the Bill in its present form practically put an end to that? Then, there is another action pending which will be ripe for trial at the fall sittings of the High Court. This action attacks the sale of the railway to the syndicate, attacks the on their bonds while the Investment Company to complete the road according to the terms of the contract, and attacks the declaration of the court cancelling the interest on their bonds while the Investment Company is in default under the contract. In this action they ask to set aside certain proceedings of the board of directors of the company, because the said board was illegally constituted directors, not having been properly qualified. Now, I say that this Bill would seriously prejudice the litigation of all the parties as it now stands.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Would the hon. member point out in what way this Bill would do more than confirm a sale that is legal in itself? It merely confirms the sale to them under the direction of the court. Would the hon. gentleman say in what way it would be a prejudice ?

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend is not so dense that he cannot see at once that the way the Bill is framed it ratifies and confirms that sale, and unless there is a saving clause it puts an end to that litigation.

If you pass legislation in this parliament, which is supreme, and if parliament ratifies, confirms and declares valid that sale, that is the end of it, that litigation is put an end to>

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Now, does the hon. gentleman think there is no question about this franchise ? Let me tell him that that matter is now pending, as I understand, before the Privy Council as to the power of the court to sell a Dominion franchise. I contend that our courts have no power in Ontario to sell. They may sell the road, the rails, the ties and the right of way, but they cannot sell a franchise which has been given by this Dominion parliament. I say that is very important. I know hon. gentlemen yvill pay no attention to this matter whatever, they will let it drift through because a majority of that committee have carelessly put in that report. I say it is most unfair and unjust that the majority of that committee, going contrary to the wishes of that committee, have put in their report, which does not even comply with the wishes of the majority.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think it is about time that hon. members should stop adopting that tone of imputing unfairness to the committee. I have distinctly stated here, and I repeat it again, that the report put in was the report agreed on by the majority of the committee, and that is the only report, there can be no other report, and there is no other report. I think it is wrong for the hon. gentleman to impute to the majority of the committee unfairness in making this report.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Well, I was not present at the final meeting of that sub-committee, but I was present at the meeting before that, and I state without any hesitation that it was the unanimous opinion of that committee that a saving clause should be inserted in this Bill, and Mr. Barwick, who represented the applicants, consented to its being in, thought it was advisable that it should be in. 1 do not know whether it is through unfairness or carelessness that that report has been put in without recommending that a saving clause should be put in the Bill. Now, whether it has been through carelessness or unfairness, we as a committee should have sense enough to see the position, and we should rectify the mistake. I am satisfied that if the other members,of the committee were here, the hon. member for Kingston (Hon. Mr. Harty), who was chairman, the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy), and the hon. member for Essex, they would say at once that this was an omission, and would wish it to be corrected. They would not take the position that the member for Yale and Cariboo is now taking and try to get this Bill through without that saving clause.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Mr. GALLIHER, I rise to a point of order. I object to the remarks of the hon. gentleman, which are uncalled for, and which do not state the facts. At the meeting prior to the last one he may have been present; I was not, and I have nothing to say about that, nor should he have anything to say about the meeting at which he was not present. If the hon. member for Essex and the hon. member for Kingston were here they would contradict the hon. member for Stormont, and they would say the report was the one adopted at the last meeting. The hon. gentleman happened to have been at one meeting too soon. He should have been at the last meeting when it was finally settled. I do not know whether it was settled by unanimous agreement at the time or not. I do not claim that. I do not state anything I do not know as a matter of personal knowledge. The hon. gentleman has undertaken to speak of something he does not know, of something that occurred at a meeting at which fie was not present.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think we are devoting far too much attention to the report of the sub-committee. The sub-committee, as I understand it, consisted of eleven members of the Railway Committee. No doubt they took this whole matter very carefully into consideration. There were three Bills before them. The report came down to the Railway Committee and I remember very well when it came before the committee making protest against its being dealt with at that time because the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) was not present and had not been heard before the Railway Committee in reference to the matter. The answer which I received was that the hon. member for Leeds was not a member of the Railway Committee, but I insisted that he should be heard notwithstanding the fact that he was not a member of the committee. There seemed to be the same disposition to force the Bill through the Railway Committee without full discussion, as there is now to force it through this committee without considering it in all its bearings. I may say that the hon. Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock) has scarcely put the case fairly in the manner in which he has presented it to the committee. The fact that these men are Americans makes no difference to me. I am prepared to deal with them just the same as if they were Canadians. He wants the committee to understand that the rights of these gentlemen who have consummated the purchase of this road should not be interfered with, that they have a fair and absolute right to the road they have purchased and that we should not compel them to pay any money in the shape of a contribution towards the settlement of these claims now pending-claims on the part of contractors or workingmen or boarding-house keepers-

because it would be taking money out of the pockets of men who have made the purchase. To my mind these men have not yet completed the purchase. X understand that the law of the country is such that their purchase will not be absolute and complete until parliament has had an opportunity of passing upon it. Therefore, the hon. Postmaster General has no right to contend that we are taking money out of the pockets of these people when we propose to attach to this legislation something that would compel the company just being incorporated by parliament to deal fairly and honourably with the creditors of the old company. It seems to me absurd that a railway forty-five miles in length should be sold for the sum of $160,000. I think that is sufficient to indicate to us that there is something wrong. It is not every workingman that can purchase a railway. I have no doubt there were workingmen who knew that the sale was to take place, but how is a workingman going to step in and protect himself when the purchase money required to be put up is $160,000 ? These men had no protection whatever. They were entirely at the mercy of the capitalists who grabbed the whole concern at what they could get it for.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: What about Mr. Cooper ? Was he not in a position to buy ?

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not know that Mr. Cooper was in a position to put up the purchase money paid for this road. I have no knowledge of his financial ability. It may be that he was not able at that time to accomplish it. However, he certainly would feel that under the law of the land, knowing that parliament would have to deal with this whole question, he, as a Canadian, understanding what his rights were, could stand on his rights and content himself with the reflection that parliament would deal fairly with him. I think he had a perfect excuse for not bidding at the sale and becoming the purchaser of a property which in all probability he did not wish to acquire. Possibly he had no desire to buy a railway, possibly it might have been a difficult matter for him to do so as it would be something he could not control. It was out of his line of business. I think, in view of what I have said that the hon. Postmaster General should not have pressed the case in the manner in which he has done, insinuating that we are doing wrong in endeavouring to take money out of the pockets of these people who had acquired the property by absolute purchase, as he would lead us to suppose, when, as a matter of fact, the purchase requires to be passed upon by this parliament.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
While listening to the laboured argument of the hon. Minister of Labour (Hon. Sir William Mulock) I endeavoured to grasp the situation and I think
he made a very important admission. He stated something to this effect : Had the old company come before this parliament and asked for the privileges that are being asked for by this new company it would have been right for parliament to have called upon them to recognize the claims of these parties who had put their money and their labour into the construction of this road.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I did not go that far.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I understood the hon. minister to make an admission to that effect.

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I tried to draw a distinction between applicants for legislation being purchasers for value, as in this case, and applicants for legislation being persons who were said to be in default. I drew a distinction between these two classes of applicants. The purchaser in this instance bought this property under the order of the court and got it free from all encumbrances, from all prior claims, and I see no connection between his status as a purchaser and the indebtedness of the former owner of the property. I do not see how, in the case of an applicant on his part, such a proposition as that which is advanced could fairly be advanced, but I wish to say that should the company itself be in default to these creditors and then apply to parliament its claims for legislation might then be considered in connection with the default of the company. We have a right to enforce equity in such a case as that, but it would be confiscation to apply such a principle, if we can call it a principle, against a purchaser, as in the present instance, applies for legislation ?

maintopic: BROCKVILLE AND SAULT STE MARIE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
It is a very important admission on the part of the hon. Minister of Labour. Where a just claim might be in existence, a moral claim, a legal claim, such a claim as it would belong to this parliament to enforce the discharge of, if it were sought simply by a change of ownership to enable a company to contract itself out of such an obligation it certainly appears to me to belong to the province of parliament to step in and protect the rights of the workingmen. Surely the rights of these men who have put their money, their labour and material into the construction of this road should be protected. The moral liability cannot have changed without the consent of the original creditors. The new company purchased only that which the old company possessed and the old company did not possess these extended franchises which they are now asking parliament to grant. This is not making a demand on the new company for concessions, nor is it an attempt to levy blackmail upon them, but it is merely a request that they shall pay the moral and just claims against the old com-

pany. The new company could only buy that which the old company had power to convey to them, and the old company had not the power to convey to them these extended privileges worth a large amount of money which they are asking parliament now to grant.

When an order of the day has been read, it must /thereupon be proceeded with, or appointed for a future day, or be discharged. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The House went into committee on Bill (No. 212) to incorporate the Alliance Bank of Canada.-Mr. Russell.

maintopic: THE ALLIANCE BANK OF CANADA.
speechtext:
On the occasion of the second reading of this Bill, I intimated to the House that I proposed at a subsequent stage to move an amendment. 1 am opposed to this Bill for special reasons, some of which I shall enumerate. I may say that I am not opposed to this Bill more than to any others of a like character which have come before the House this session, but I am opposed to it because I believe we are going too far in chartering hanks. We have already passed through the various stages some seven bank charters this session, and these have received the assent of His Excellency. Two more are on the Order Paper, which will make a total of nine new bank charters enacted this session To my mind that increase is uncalled for.' No less a financial authority than Mr. Fyshe, the general manager of the Merchants Bank of Canada, in his last annual statement to the shareholders, says, speaking of new bank charters, that he regards

the course which parliament is pursuing as being unwise.

maintopic: THE ALLIANCE BANK OF CANADA.
speechtext: If my hon. friend will allow me, I would point out that as the hon. member who has charge of this Bill is not present, we had better not proceed with it unless my hon. friend's remarks are simply of a general nature.

maintopic: THE ALLIANCE BANK OF CANADA.
speechtext: The exception I take to the passage of this Bill is the same as I would take to the passage of any other Bill of a like character. It is stated that Mr. Eyshe, general manager of the Merchants Bank of Canada has expressed the opinion that there is no more use for these new banks in Canada than there is for a fifth wheel to a coach, which is a very strong expression coming from such an eminent financial authority. For my part, I regard all these new banks simply as so many new channels through which money is sent out of Canada instead of bringing more money into Canada, and consequently the more banks we have, the more means we have of sending money out of the country to find investment elsewhere. I do not propose for one moment to say that it is not quite proper for our chartered banks to hold a healthy reserve in some large financial centre, such as New York, where money can be called on in case of emergency and be obtained on very short notice ; but it is a well known fact that what has for years been regarded as a healthy reserve in a large financial centre has now become a large business investment. Taking the May statement of our chartered banks, I find that at the end of May, they had invested in American securities no less a sum than $102,000,000. On call loan outside of Canada, $38,000,000 ; current loans also outside of Canada, $27,000,000 ; and on railway stocks, bonds and debentures, $37,000,000, largely American, making a total of $102,000,000, practically invested in American securities outside of Canada. Or equal to sixteen per cent of the total assets of all the banks of Canada ; or $26,000,000 more than the entire paid up capital of all our chartered banks ; or $44.000,000 more than the entire currency issued by the chartered banks. To my mind, this is too great. I may say that during the month of June the banks, for some good reason, possibly because of the disturbance in financial circles, especially in the province of Ontario, called in current loans outside of Canada for no less a sum than $5,000,000. The sum I have named, $102,000,000, does not include loans on stock and bonds in Canada, $44,000,000, which are believed to be very largely, at any rate a considerable portion of them, on American securities. This is a heavy drain of money from Canada to the ^ United States, and it discriminates against the Canadian borrower. It enhances the cost of money to the farmer who wants

maintopic: THE ALLIANCE BANK OF CANADA.
speechtext:
to borrow money to buy a farm, improve his buildings or add to his stock. It enhances the cost of money to the manufacturer engaged in the industries of the country. It enhances the cost of money to the business man who wishes to use it in his trade. It enhances the cost of money to business men who wish to use it for the purpose of moving the crops for which purpose a very large sum of money will very shortly be required. It increases the cost of money for our public works, for the improvement of transportation. In short, it enhances the cost of money all along the line.
Banks are simply the creatures of parliament. They are not created for the benefit of shareholders alone. If they were, this would be quite a proper thing to allow the banks to do. But banks are created for the benefit of the people at large as well as for the benefit of the shareholder, and they are expected, in return for the advantages and special privileges they have received, to furnish the capital necessary for trading purposes in the country. Banks enjoy very special privileges, privileges which no other incorporated companies in this country enjoy. They are permitted to float their, promissory notes as currency to the extent of their paid up capital, which, at the present time, amounts to about $75,000,000. Practically they are authorized by parliament to borrow from the people $75,000,000 without interest, and every dollar of these notes is guaranteed by the parliament of Canada and is as good as gold. Banks, then, we say, should aid the business of the country; it is their business so to do in return for the special privileges they enjoy. They should always give the preference to home investment rather than to foreign investments. The amendment I propose has as its object to limit the investments of our banks in American securities. And this is proposed for two purposes-first, in order to keep capital in Canada and aid Canadian enterprise; second, to minimize the improper dealing in stocks of which so much has been said so very recently. This. I believe, would be the result if our banks were prohibited from investing so largelv in American stocks. It is the fact, I believe, that this business of dealing in margin could not be carried to the extent it is, were it not for the help of our banks. The chartered banks of Canada advance very large sums of money on the security of American stocks, stocks used for speculative purposes. They advance, possibly, to the extent of seventy-five per cent, in which case the broker is only called upon, in purchasing the stocks for speculative purposes, to put up twenty-five per cent. Now, my desire would be that this order should be reversed and so make it difficult for the brokers to carry on business, that is, those who are engaged in the illegitimate business of stock speculation. I would make them

put up the seventy-five per cent and allow them to call upon the bank only for the twenty-five per cent. If this were done, we shall have a more healthful condition of things in our country. It would minimize the dealing in stocks on margin which has received so much attention and which has caused so much misery and loss in Canada during the present season. The amendment I propose may be said not to go far enough. I simply propose that it should be left to the shareholders to say whether or not the bank shall be permitted to invest money in American stocks of this character. But I believe that if the matter is left in the hands of the shareholders, they will control the investment in foreign securities and will see to it that the directors are prevented from putting up such large sums of money on American stocks and bonds as the bank returns of the present time show that our banks are doing. If the committee adopts the clauses of this Bill I shall then propose my amendment as a new clause to be added to the Bill. I shall read the amendment now, in order that the committee may be seized of it:-
Notwithstanding anything contained in the Bank Act, the said bank shall not, either directly or indirectly, lend money or make advances upon the security of, or take as collateral security for any loan made by it, the bonds, stocks and other securities or obligations of any company or corporation or body corporate not incorporated by the parliament of Great Britain, or by the parliament of Canada, or of a province of Canada, until the consent thereto by the shareholdors of said bank shall have been obtained at a special meeting of the said bank specially called for that purpose.

maintopic: THE ALLIANCE BANK OF CANADA.
speechtext:
I did not know that this subject was coming up, but, as it is before us, I desire to say something about the influence of our banks. There are a great many who declare that our banking system is perhaps the best in the world, I confess I never agreed with that view. I am free to admit that our banking system has very many good elements and serves very many good purposes. But I cannot regard as the best that can be devised a banking system which does not provide for receiving the deposits of the labouring class of the people, and making money available for the same class when need arises. Comparatively speaking there is a very small minority of the people of the country who are able to avail themselves to-day of the banks when they require to raise money. I have always thought that If banks were so arranged as to supply the needs of the country, they would provide means for carrying on the commercial operations and Industrial pursuits in every locality where the earnings of the people have enabled them to put money away In a savings institution. It is true we have a pretty fair supply of banks to-day. I agree with the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) that we have enough standard banks in the country to do
the financial work of the country to-day; therefore, there is no urgent need, in my judgment for passing this proposed charter to establish another bank. We need more hanks, but not of the class of those we have now.
Why is it that these banks do not fulfil the needs of the people ? Let me give an example. We have a standard bank in the country, and those who are fortunate enough to save a little money put It away In that bank. Take a radius of ten or twenty miles, in the centre of which district there is a bank. Deposits are made in that bank. What becomes of that money ? As soon as it accumulates in that bank, which is probably a branch of another standard bank, with its headquarters in Montreal or Toronto, a request is made that that money be sent to headquarters, and after it gets to headquarters, then where does it go ? As the hon. member for Halton says, it is invested in stocks or bonds in the city of New York, or Chicago, or some other place. That, in my judgment, is not what the hank is intended for. The money does not serve the best purpose which it can serve in this country. That money should be kept for the needs of the locality where the people have earned it and saved it, and it should be available in that locality for the purpose of other industrial pursuits, to give employment to the labouring men there. The money was earned there and saved by the people in that locality, therefore, it ought to be available for the needs of the people to start other industrial pursuits, and to carry them on, so as to give more employment to labour and enable others to earn more money. But If you want to get that money back again, you cannot do it, because the security necessary to furnish is such that poor people cannot supply it. Therefore, the money is not available to them, but it is available for the wealthy, for those who have at their hand ample security to offer to the banks. The great majority of the people cannot provide that security, therefore, the banks do not afford them facilities for the use of the money that they are justly entitled to, andv the money is invested elsewhere.
What we need, in my judgment, is some species of saving banks in which small savings of labourers, of farmers and of poor people can be deposited, and of which they can borrow small amounts for short periods. Our banking system at present does not afford for the poor people such facilities. Is there any country where the banking system does provide such facilities ? I think the banking system of Germany provides them. And I am told that right here in the province of Quebec, that is not supposed to be so brilliant in the financial world, they havei these very small banks, savings banks, which are called co-operative banks, where may be received the savings of the lower classes for whatever

radius is chosen to be specified in that corporation, where are received the savings of the people in that locality and from whicli the people can draw small sums in case of need, to pay for rent, if you like, to make payments on life insurance, or the other needs of life. They can go to that institution and borrow money from time to time and make their payments. A great majority of men can earn money, and if they could hand it over to some corporation or some individual to finance it and save it for them, and loan it out to them again when they need it, they would be in a very much better position than they are to-day. They are economical and frugal enough to save money, but they cannot finance it and invest it; if they attempt to do so, they are likely to lose it. Now if there were provided some co-operative banking institutions where the money can be handed over in small sums of five cents and upwards by depositors, letting some other more competent person invest the money for them, and from which they can borrow small amounts when they are required to meet the urgent needs of life, X say that such a banking system would meet the wants of the common people far better than any we have to-day. The difficulty is that we have not got enough of them. There are banks for the wealthy, banks for the rich; for the millionaire, but there are not enough banks for the poor people of the country. The majority of the people are poor, and, therefore, they require banking facilities of a different nature from those required by rich men.
Now, to provide for urgent needs, what takes place ? We have our private banks. These private banks will charge a rate of Interest running from eight to twelve per cent, and sometimes as high as twenty per cent. Ten and twelve per cent is the ordinary rate of interest paid in these private banks. Why do these private banks flourish to-day, notwithstanding that they do not afford any great security to the depositors ? It is because that class of poor people can avail themselves of these banks to borrow money which they cannot do from a standard bank. They are obliged to pay a larger rate of interest, but they will pay it, and, therefore, these private banks flourish where a standard bank cannot get business enough to keep it going. We see that all over this country. I take an example in the village where I live. There are two private banks flourishing for years, and it is only within the last few years that a standard bank was established there. I am within the mark when I say that forty or fifty farmers and poor people go to these private banks to borrow money for one who goes to the standard bank, who never go into that standard bank to do any business whatever, becaiise they cannot go there and get the money in small sums for their needs without offering

maintopic: THE ALLIANCE BANK OF CANADA.
speechtext: security that they are unable to give. Being unable to offer the security required by the standard bank, they go to the private bank, where they are obliged to pay a much higher rate of interest perhaps than their earnings would justify. But they are obliged to pay it because they can get the accommodation there which the standard bank denies them. I say we have enough of that class of banks to-day. They are, as my hon. friend from Halton says, institutions started for the purpose of taking the earnings of people that are deposited in banks to invest them outside the country, instead of keeping them for reinvestment in the industrial needs of the locality where the money has been earned. This money is invested in railway stocks, in bonds and mortgages belonging outside the country, consequently it is of very little advantage to the country where it has been earned. Until we devise a banking system that will reach a larger number of poor people, I am not in favour of giving any more charters for new banks. But I am at any time willing to give a charter to a bank that will accommodate the great bulk of the people in the manner I have mentioned, that will put within the reach of the poor man, the labouring man, the servant girl, if you like, the small farmer if you like, the man who has not the security to offer that a standard bank requires facilities for depositing small sums and borrowing small sums, where people can get accommodation in small amounts that will enable them to tide over the emergencies of life, and in which they can deposit their small savings.

maintopic: THE ALLIANCE BANK OF CANADA.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think there is another side to this question that hon. gentlemen are leaving out of sight altogether. I know on good authority that the banks of the country are willing and ready to lend money on securities for the transaction of the business and carrying on the enterprises of this country. The reason they are not doing it seems to me to be wrapped up in the fiscal policy of the country. The reason why money is going out to the United States is because the industries are protected there and the money seeks the country where industries are protected. The United States have a stable tariff protective policy, and the reason why our money is going to the United States is because they are building up their industries. Our millions are sent over to the American banks to be invested there and they are bringing a more profitable return than they can bring here.

maintopic: THE ALLIANCE BANK OF CANADA.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him one question?

maintopic: THE ALLIANCE BANK OF CANADA.
speechtext: The hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Johnston) can talk when I am through.

maintopic: THE ALLIANCE BANK OF CANADA.
speechtext: I was just going to ask the hon. gentleman one question.	_

maintopic: THE ALLIANCE BANK OF CANADA.
speechtext: If we had a stable protective policy established in this country, so that our industries could be built up, and so that capital would be invested, the banks of the country would be ready and willing to lend money to these enterprises, and our millions would be used here in the feeding of our people and the building up of our cities. I do not want to enter upon a tariff discussion, but the whole banking system and the question of the security upon which the banks will lend their money is wrapped up in the question of the stability of the enterprises of the country which in turn depend upon tariff protection and tariff stability, and you cannot carry on the enterprises of the country when the ministry are handing out the hybrid policy of protecting our industries by bonuses and such hand to mouth expedients that the business people of the country have no dependence upon. I do not know whether the government's policy is to be continued on the basis of the numerous fiscal changes that were advocated during the 18 years that hon. gentlemen opposite were in opposition. What we want is a stable policy that the people can depend upon, and if we had that the money of the country would be invested in Canada.

maintopic: THE ALLIANCE BANK OF CANADA.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before you leave the Chair, I beg to move that
Notwithstanding anything contained in the Bank Aot, the said bank shall not, either directly or indirectly, lend money or make advances upon the security of, or .take as collateral security for .any loan made by it, the bonds, stocks and other securities or obligations of any company or corporation or body corporate not incorporated by the parliament of Great Britain, or by the parliament of Canada, or ol a province of Canada, until the consent thereto by the shareholders of .said bank shall have been obtained at a special meeting of the said bank specially called for that purpose.

maintopic: THE ALLIANCE BANK OF CANADA.
speechtext: Surely we are not going to begin at this stage to get in a general principle, if it is a general principle, which will destroy this bank. I know some of the men who are in the bank. The very name of Mr. John F. Stairs should be sufficient for hon. gentlemen opposite, and to handicap a bank at the start while all other banks have no such handicap whatever is the wrong,way to get at it. If the hon. gentleman thinks the banking system is not right why does he not submit a general proposition to amend the Banking Act, instead of just at the end of a Bill incorporating a company composed of such gentlemen as these are. headed by Mr. Stairs, proposing an amendment which will destroy the usefulness of the bank.

maintopic: THE ALLIANCE BANK OF CANADA.
speechtext:
In answer to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fraser), I would say that I
am no respecter of persons. Mr. Stairs may
be a very excellent man. I have no doubt he is. I have no doubt he is a very respectable man, but I am not dealing with men ; I am dealing with the principle which I have enunciated, and which I contend I am correct in stating. The hon. gentleman complains that I have moved this amendment to a special charter. 1 may say that I am prepared to support a similar amendment to all other charters, and I shall give the hon. gentleman an opportunity to-morrow if he desires to support an amendment to the Banking Act, of which I have given notice, and which has been on the paper for some time, until I would ascertain how the House would deal with this question. If the hon. gentleman is in favour of applying the same principle to all chartered banks, I would be very happy to give him an opportunity of seconding the Bill which I propose to introduce along lines similar to what I propose to-night, so that I think that objection should be dropped. Now, it is a common plan to establish a principle by attacking individual cases. I think we frequently do that. I do not see any other way in which I can reach it. It is not possible for me to amend the Banking Act unless I have the consent of the government, because the time for moving an amendment of that kind in so far as this session is concerned, is passed, but it is within my power to move an amendment to a private Bill, and declare a principle that I believe is a proper principle in connection with the banking system. Now,
I can only say that if tlie hon. gentleman will secure the support of the government for an amendment to the Banking Act I will be very happy to give him an opportunity of supporting it.

maintopic: THE ALLIANCE BANK OF CANADA.
speechtext:
I could not ask the government to support such an amendment, because I do not believe in it. Certainly I am not in sympathy with the hon. gentleman. I think the banking system of this country is the best in the world, and when I heard an hon. gentleman saying that our money goes to the banks of the United States because their banks are better than ours, I thought it was one of the most laughable things I had ever beard in this parliament, because the stability of the banking system of Canada is the envy of the United States, and there is no banking system in the world better than ours, not even that of the motherland.
Amendment negatived, and section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

speechtext: It is quite difficult to understand the persistent opposition of my hon. friend from West Toronto to this charter. Before the Bill was submitted to the committee, he was supplied with a copy of it, so that he might consult with the solicitor of the city of Toronto to see that all its interests had been provided for and safeguarded. The consideration of the Bill was deferred for three or four sittings of the committee to enable the hon. gentleman and the solicitor of the city of Toronto to prepare such amendments as they might think necessary to safeguard the interests of the municipality. Certain amendments were submitted by the solicitor, and they were all agreed to, with the exception of this one, which the company and its promoters felt that they could not accept, as it would handicap the company to such an extent that the charter would be worthless to it, inasmuch as the hon. gentleman proposes to make it complusory on this company to enter into agreements with other companies which have been heretofore incorporated, while there is no compulsion on the small companies now looking for incorporation. It is permissive on the one side, but compulsory on the other. It is jug-handled legislation, which it seems to me is inconsistent with the position the hon. gentleman has taken with regard to the monopoly of the Bell Telephone Company. Here is a company which is represented by its promoters as willing to invest its capital to the extent of $20,000,000 or $25,000,000, and if the committee accept the amendment of the hon. member for West Toronto, it will make their charter of little or no value.

maintopic: CANADIAN TELEPHONE AND TELEGRAPH COMPANY.
speechtext:
The object of this amendment is to provide that, at the option of other telephone companies, this company shall, on such other companies granting it similar terms and conditions, permit connections to be made with its wires, and messages to be delivered over them. It primarily affects only this company, and is not general legislation. This company has not yet any legal status ; and, in view of the experience which the people of Canacla have had with the Bell Telephone Company, which has persistently refused to give connection with smaller independent companies, it has been thought that if we are to have competition in telephony in Canada, we should embrace the opportunity which is afforded by this Bill to ask that this important and much-desired amendment should be made in the charter of this company. Other companies may take advantage of this clause : but they must subject themselves

to its entire provisions before they can avail themselves of any advantages under it; and no jurisdiction is given to the Governor in Council unless there is a dispute between the parties as to the terms and conditions under which the mutual service is to be rendered. I think I can appeal to the sense of this committee that the time has come when there must be some improvement made in the methods by which the telephone companies are conducted. There can be no question of the necessity for some such provision unless competition in telephony is to be an absurd farce. Local telephone companies have from time to time been incorporated in different sections of the country only to fail one after the other ; and the reason of their failure has been that they have not been able to get exchange messages over the trunk lines. There have been a good many objections made to the proposed amendment. It is said that we are adding to a Private Bill a general section which should apply to all companies. But, as I have pointed out, the provisions of this clause affect only this company primarily, and other companies which may voluntarily desire to take advantage of it. The other companies must give a mutual service if they desire to take advantage of the use of this company's wires for the purpose of exchanging messages. They must be prepared to give this company equal facilities over their lines. The matter was discussed a good deal when the Bill was before the committee. I have the greatest possible respect for my hon. friend from Ottawa, and I desire to assure him that the interests of the municipalities generally are what I am trying to safeguard and promote, and not the interests of one municipality in particular. The hon. member will remember that this clause was submitted on behalf of the Union of Canadian Municipalities. It was acceptable to and accepted by them. It has met with strenuous opposition, it is true, from the company which has practically a monopoly of telephony in most of the provinces of Canada. It does not affect that company in the slightest degree directly. It does not affect any other company which is in existence to-day unless that company may desire to take advantage of its provisions. It is meeting with a great deal of objection from the Bell Telephone Company, because, assuming this enterprise to be a bona fide one, if it were obliged to give an interchange of messages with the smaller companies, especially the farmers' companies, for twelve months or two years, the Bell Telephone Company would be obliged to give a similar service, and what is now a grinding monopoly would be practically broken down. Hon. gentlemen who make use of the argument that we should provide general legislation, and should cover all companies under such general legislation, do not need to be reminded that last year and this year attempts have
been made to provide for the case of the Bell Telephone Company and all other companies doing business in Canada. That Bill has not made very satisfactory progress so far. It was introduced in the House and referred to the Railway Committee, and by that committee referred to a sub-committee. We have practically done nothing at the meetings of the sub-committee except listen to the arguments of counsel against the provisions of the Bill. If hon. gentlemen who object to this clause will give us some guarantee that the Bill to which I refer will be taken up by the government and enacted into law, the insertion of clause 22 is not so urgent; but as there is very little hope that that will be done, I propose to test the feeling of the committee. It is essential, in the interest of telephone users, that tne monopoly should be broken down. That great monopoly, the Bell Company, is not affected directly by the operation of this clause. It can be only interfered with indirectly ; and if interfered with at all, that interference will be in the public interest. I ask for this clause the respectful consideration of the committee, not because it is intended to benefit one locality, but because it will be a substantial advantage to all municipalities where local services are in operation, and will eventually compel all telephone companies to give similar service over their lines to that which we seek to compel this company to give.
Mr, LENNOX. I would not oppose the Bill in its present form did I not believe it my duty to do so in the interests of the people generally. While it is desirable to do all we possibly can to encourage the incorporation of this company because it tends to break down an injurious monopoly, yet, on the other hand, we should be careful to avoid being again met with the question of vested rights and should secure all the advantage we can to the people by providing for a free interchange of messages. Therefore I feel bound to support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Clark). The strongest argument that I heard in opposition to the incorporation of this company was that it would compel merchants and others doing business with the public to have two instruments in their places of business and) pay for two services., That seemed to me a very formidable objection, and therefore I have great pleasure in supporting this amendment, which will, to a large extent, enable us to overcome that difficulty. I have no doubt that this is a Bill which has been pretty fully considered by members of the committee. It has attracted a good deal of attention, and therefore, I need not elaborate at all the reasons why I propose to support this amendment. The hon. member who moved the amendment has not as yet spoken of one portion of it, and I would therefore mention it now. As the clause

now stands, it reads :	* The company may
enter into agreements or arrangements.' The words 1 and shall ' were struck out in committee and I am unable to see any special benefit in clause twenty-two if we strike out these words. In dealing with this, company, which has as yet no special rights, we are entitled to ask for whatever is in the interests of the people and insist upon such conditions as we deem necessary. I see very good reasons why, in granting this charter, we should: make this clause twenty-two compulsory. We should provide that upon request being made for an exchange of messages upon reciprocal or mutual terms, this company will be bound to comply with that request. The junior member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) who made a very eloquent speech on this question, claimed that this was spoliation.

The hon. member (Mr. Fraser) compels me to say more. The hon. member for Ottawa made a most violent speech. He claimed that it was an outrage on the rights of the people. After he had read the clause, he had to vary his opinions to some extent. He had to come within the lines of reason, and I trust he will not again advance any such outrageous arguments. This company has only such rights as are consistent with the general interets of the public. The argument that we should embody this, not in a special Act but a general Act, would be very well, if there were a general Act before this parliament; but if we allow this opportunity to go and leave the matter over until another session, we will meet a much more strenuous opposition. We will have the combined opposition of the Bell Telephone Company and this new company, which will probably be a strong organization by that time, and will find much more difficulty in dealing with this question. Some hon. gentlemen are fond of pointing out that this is special legislation, and the hon. gentleman who called my attention to being wrong a moment ago is not one of those who do not, at times, resort to that line of argument. When we find out that a certain system which has prevailed for years is not working satisfactorily and that the consensus of opinion is that a new system should be encouraged, the sooner we apply a remedy the better.
Therefore, on whatever occasion it arises I see no objection. When parties come and ask for privileges which are, to some extent, antagonistic to the general interest Mr. LENNOX.
-that is the time to exact the terms by which those to whom these privileges are given shall be guided. Now, it is said that the second clause proposed in connection with 22 is unfair to this company. We ask in the event of the other company being willing to enter into an agreement to make it compulsory upon this company to enter into an arrangement satisfactory to the Governor in Council: I see no unfairness at all about it. If we were to say that this company must transmit the message of some other company over their line and give them no similar rights against the other companies, or if we were to compel them to carry these messages without being paid, as my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) suggests, it would be unfair. But we simply provide that they shall make such an arrangement as may be approved by the Governor in Council. Upon the whole, not going into more details, I wish to say that I believe it is wise at this time to have this legislation. And I hope the gentlemen who see the importance of having a general scheme enacted will support this amendment, for I believe we will find that it will be greatly to the advantage of the people generally and that at another session, instead of being confronted by a combination of two large companies, we shall have an illustration of the beneficial working of this new arrangement, and by next session we shall secure it as a general measure governing all telephone companies throughout the country.

maintopic: CANADIAN TELEPHONE AND TELEGRAPH COMPANY.
speechtext:
This company, when it applied for an Act of incorporation, very good naturedly accepted many of the proposed amendments to their Bill. The experience of years have proven the objections to the other company. One of those objections was their forcing their way through municipalities regardless of the rights of the corporations to control or to impose terms. This company very graciously accepted an amendment providing for that, and thereby satisfied the requirements of the representatives of the municipal corporations. They accepted everything till it came to this proposed amendment. Serious objection was raised to this, and it does seem to me that this is the only proposed amendment against which serious objection could be raised. One objection was that if you compel this company to arrange with all other companies, you may compel them to arrange with small companies whose lines are not well built or well maintained, and the large company will be the one to receive the blame for inefficient service. It seems to me that this could be overcome with a little ingenuity. I would suggest a provision to compel this company to exchange messages with other companies having lines built and maintained according to a certain standard. With such a provision, I.think there would be little difficulty in carrying out the main

idea. But if you leave this Bill without amendment, you leave it with the most objectionable feature of the Bell Telephone Company to-day. We have private companies establishing lines in many different places throughout the country. I take as an example the county In which I live.
1 can count, from memory, about eighteen different private lines there, not one of which is allowed to connect with the Bell Telephone lines or exchange messages with it. It would be a great convenience if they could do so, and it is because they cannot that there is such a strong objection to the Bell Telephone Company. That company is regarded as a soulless monopoly. It does not make an effort to serve the wants of the people. It was because of this very objection that we had all the excitement raised over the line in East York, where they would not allow the instrument of the private line to be put in the railway station because of the arrangement giving an exclusive privilege to the Bell Telephone Company. The same difficulty exists all over the country, and it is because of this that there is a burning desire for competition. When this company proposed to secure a charter and establish competition, every one was anxious that the charter should go through. But when they refuse to exchange messages with other companies, we do not look upon the enterprise with the same favour we did before. Without such a condition, it would be very little better than the Bell Telephone Company. An hon. friend says that it is uo better than the Bell Telephone Company. I think it is, and for this reason. This Bill provides that they shall not go into a municipality except upon terms acceptable to the municipal corporation. That is better than the Bell Telephone Company will do. Ihere are many other provisions which this company has accepted which the Bell Telephone Company would not accept. But if they will not give us the advantage of the long distance telephone, we shall be stin in the hands of the Bell monopoly the users of private lines will be no better ott than they are to-day. It is desirable, theie-fore that this clause should become law. If it' does, I would suggest that there might be a limit, that this company shall not be compelled to exchange messages with lines which do not maintain their lines in a cei-tain state of efficiency.	_

Mr. CLARKE moved that the Bill be not now read the third time, but that it be referred back to Committee of the Whole House with instructions to strike out Clause 22 and insert the following in lieu thereof.
The company may- and shall enter into agreements or arrangements with any other telephone or telegraph companies now or hereafter incorporated for the transmission nr forwarding of the messages or despatches of such ether companies, or of the subscribers to or users thereof, upon the lines of, or by the company to the place of destination of such messages or despatches, and for a division or apportionment of the tolls or rates in respect of such transmission or forwarding, provided such other companies are willing to enter into like agreements or arrangements with the company for the transmission or forwarding of the messages or despatches of the company or of the subscribers or users thereof, and for a like division or apportionment of the tolls or rates.
2. In the event of the company being unwilling or failing to enter into agreements or arrangements with any other such companies so willing as aforesaid, or in the event of any such agreements or arrangements when made being unsatisfactory to the Governor in Council, the Governor in Council may, from time to time, make such reciprocal provisions, applying to the company and such other companies, as he deems equitable and proper for such transmission or forwarding, iand the company and such other companies shall be bound by and shall carry out such agreements or arrangements or such provisions, as the case may be, and /upon any violation thereof shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding one hundred dollars for each such violation.
